idiom_name: internal monitor over a sealed operation hierarchy with an exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Two language features carry the classic structure. internal visibility is enforced by the compiler and limited to the module the declaration is compiled with - a Gradle source set, with the documented exception that the test source set may see main's internals - so the monitor and its state can be kept out of the public API of the module. A sealed class or interface fixes the set of direct subclasses at compile time, so a when expression over the operation hierarchy is checked for exhaustiveness and a new operation cannot be added without the monitor being updated; that makes the enumeration of mediated operations a compile-time property, which is a real contribution to the verifiability requirement. The module boundary is not a security boundary on the JVM: reflection with setAccessible, agents and --add-opens reach internal and private members, so tamper resistance still comes from the deployment.
pitfalls: internal is module-wide, not monitor-only: any code in the same Gradle module may call it, and the test source set is explicitly allowed to see main's internals - so the boundary has to be drawn by module structure, not by the modifier alone.
Default visibility is public: a declaration without a modifier is visible everywhere, which is how a mediated operation accidentally leaves the module.

Sealed-ness is not transitive: a direct subclass that is not itself sealed can be extended freely, so an operation hierarchy meant to stay closed needs sealed at every level or the when stops being exhaustive.
JVM reflection and instrumentation reach private and internal members regardless of Kotlin's checks; the monitor needs the container or process boundary to resist code you do not trust.
